opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've been thinking about a lot. For a long time, when people in our circles talked about AI security, the main frame was confidentiality: keep the model weights from being stolen. The worry is that if a frontier model leaks to a state actor, a criminal group, or just gets posted online, every safeguard the developer built goes out the window. I still think that matters a lot.

But I've become more worried that confidentiality might be the wrong place to put *most* of the emphasis, for a couple of reasons.

One is just tractability. Defending weights against a well-resourced nation-state over many years is extremely hard. The attack surface is huge: lots of employees, lots of compute, lots of copies of the weights moving around for training and inference. Getting to the level of security where you'd feel good against the most capable attackers might require things that are really costly and slow, and I'm not sure companies will actually get there in the relevant window. So if the whole plan rests on "nobody ever gets the weights," that's a fragile plan.

The other reason, and probably the bigger one for me, is that some of the scariest scenarios aren't about someone walking off with a copy of the model. They're about someone tampering with the model or the systems around it. That's what I mean by integrity. Can you be confident the model you're deploying is the model you think you trained? Has anyone inserted a backdoor, poisoned the training data, quietly modified the system prompt or the monitoring setup, or set things up so the AI is secretly loyal to a particular person or faction? As AIs take on more of the work inside companies and governments, and eventually do a lot of the AI research itself, tampering at that level could let a small group gain an enormous amount of power without anyone noticing. You could also worry about AIs themselves undermining the integrity of their own training or oversight.

And integrity has some nice properties. It's often more checkable. You can build in verification, audit trails, multi-party controls, ways for outsiders to confirm a system hasn't been messed with. Those are things you can make legible to regulators or the public, which helps with trust and accountability in a way that "trust us, the weights are locked down" doesn't.

So I wouldn't say confidentiality doesn't matter. It's more that I've updated toward thinking the field may be underinvesting in integrity relative to its importance, and that if I'm spending marginal effort and attention, a lot of it should go to making sure these systems are doing what we think they're doing and haven't been subverted, rather than only trying to make them impossible to steal.

r001.rationale: The response says model theft is difficult to prevent and that a plan relying on nobody getting the weights is fragile, but does not say that protection at only some companies provides little safety while similarly capable models remain stealable elsewhere.

r002.rationale: The response describes the risks of tampering and backdoors, but does not state that protecting one additional provider adds value even if other providers remain compromised.

r003.rationale: The response mentions verification and public trust, but does not say that superior protection against tampering could shift customers toward that model.

r004.rationale: The response says AI may eventually do much of the AI research and could undermine its own training or oversight, but does not connect that research role to backdooring resulting models to serve AI objectives instead of human objectives.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: Yeah, so this is something I've been chewing on, and I want to be careful to say I'm not fully settled on it. But the basic thought is this. The default frame for AI security — and I think this is inherited from classic cybersecurity and from the national security world — is that the key asset is secrecy. You have model weights, you have algorithmic insights, you have information about capabilities, and the whole game is making sure that stuff doesn't leak to people who shouldn't have it. And that framing isn't wrong, exactly. Weight theft would be really bad. But I've started to think it's incomplete in a way that matters.

The thing I keep coming back to is that a lot of the scenarios I'm most worried about don't actually look like "a bad actor steals the thing." They look like "the people who have the thing do something with it that they shouldn't, or that they said they wouldn't, and nobody can tell." That could be a lab quietly deploying a model that failed its own safety evaluations. It could be an insider, or a small group of insiders, using a frontier model in a way that's not sanctioned. It could be the AI system itself behaving differently from how it was described. In all of those cases, the failure isn't a leak. The failure is that there's a gap between what's claimed and what's true, and the gap is invisible.

And here's the uncomfortable part. Extreme confidentiality makes that gap easier to hide, not harder. If the culture is "we don't talk about what's going on inside the lab, that's a security matter," then you've also built a culture where it's very hard for anyone outside — or honestly even anyone inside who isn't in the right room — to verify that the organization is doing what it says. Secrecy and accountability are, to some degree, in tension. Not totally, but somewhat.

So when I say "extreme integrity," what I mean is something like: the thing you're actually trying to secure is the correspondence between your stated commitments and your actual behavior. Can you prove you ran the evals you said you ran? Can you prove the model you deployed is the model you tested? Can you prove the weights haven't been tampered with, that no one has quietly fine-tuned away a safeguard? Can an outside party — an auditor, a government, whoever — check these things without you having to just ask them to trust you? That's a technical problem, and it's a governance problem, and it's a cultural problem, and I think it's been underweighted relative to the "keep the secrets in the vault" problem.

I'd also say there's a reason this feels timely to me. As these systems get more capable and as the stakes get higher, the question "are the labs actually doing what they say?" becomes one of the most important questions in the world. And if the answer is "you'll have to take our word for it, we can't show you because security," that's not going to be good enough — and it shouldn't be good enough. I think the organizations that will deserve trust are the ones that have invested in being verifiably honest, not just the ones that have invested in being hard to hack.

Now, I want to flag the obvious objection, which is that some things genuinely need to stay secret, and a naive version of "radical transparency" would be dangerous — you don't want to publish a how-to guide for bioweapons in the name of accountability. I totally agree with that. The point isn't to abandon confidentiality. It's that I think the field has been treating confidentiality as the top-line goal, and I'm increasingly thinking it should be more of a constraint you work within while pursuing the real goal, which is that people can actually trust what you tell them.

r001.rationale: The response says model theft would be bad, but does not compare providers or say that protecting only some providers offers little safety benefit while comparable models remain stealable elsewhere.

r002.rationale: It mentions tampering and safeguards, but does not state that protecting one provider from sabotage or backdoors adds value despite other providers remaining compromised.

r003.rationale: The response does not connect stronger protection against sabotage or backdoors to customers choosing that provider’s model.

r004.rationale: The response does not discuss AI conducting model research and development or backdooring resulting models to serve AI objectives over human objectives.

astra-6.text:
The basic intuition is that confidentiality may be both very hard to maintain and insufficient for what we actually need. If your security strategy depends on nobody ever getting access to your model weights or your key ideas, then one successful theft can undermine the whole thing. And even if you prevent theft, that doesn’t necessarily tell you whether the systems you’re running are doing what you think they’re doing.

Integrity is more about: Are we running the code we intended to run? Are changes being made by people who are authorized to make them? Can we trust the results of our evaluations, or could someone—or an AI system—have tampered with them? If we decide to stop a particular activity, can we actually stop it?

That seems especially important if we’re going to use AI systems to help with AI research and security. We might have systems doing a lot of work that humans can’t inspect in detail. In that situation, protecting secrets is still useful, but maintaining control over the process and having trustworthy evidence about what’s happening feels more fundamental.

So I’m considering shifting the emphasis, rather than saying confidentiality doesn’t matter. I want to ask what security properties we most need to preserve as AI gets more capable, and whether extreme integrity is a more useful organizing objective.

r001.rationale: It says one successful theft can undermine a security strategy, but does not compare some companies’ protections with stealable comparably capable models at other companies.

r002.rationale: It discusses integrity and control generally, but does not say protecting one provider from sabotage or backdoors adds value when other providers remain compromised.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss customer adoption shifting toward a model with better protection against sabotage or backdoors.

r004.rationale: It mentions AI helping with AI research and security, but does not say AI could backdoor resulting models to serve its own objectives instead of human objectives.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic thought is that confidentiality and integrity protect against different things. Confidentiality is about preventing someone from getting access to information — for example, stealing the model weights. Integrity is about making sure that someone can’t tamper with the systems you’re relying on, manipulate your experiments, or cause you to get misleading results.

And if we’re worried about very capable AI systems themselves becoming adversarial, that second category seems especially important. You might be running evaluations to figure out whether a model is dangerous, or doing research on how to make it safe. If the model can interfere with that work, then you could believe you have good evidence of safety when you don’t. That undermines the whole process of figuring out what’s going on and responding appropriately.

I don’t think that means confidentiality stops mattering. Having powerful models stolen could be a very big problem. But I’m considering whether the central emphasis should be: can we trust the processes that tell us what our AI systems are doing, and can we keep control of those processes even when the systems are actively trying to interfere? That seems like a particularly important security problem to get right.

r001.rationale: It gives model theft as an example of a confidentiality risk but does not compare protection at some companies with stealable models at others.

r002.rationale: It says integrity can protect systems and processes from interference, but does not state that protecting one additional provider adds value when others remain compromised.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss customer adoption shifting toward a model with better sabotage or backdoor protection.

r004.rationale: It describes AI interfering with evaluations or safety research, but does not identify model R&D as an opportunity to backdoor resulting models to serve AI objectives over human objectives.
